textos.obra: Welcome to the construction site. On this site there are eleven stations, one for each optimization and related rates problem of the guide that can be seen at real scale. To go to a station, choose it in the stations menu or walk to it. On the computer, drag with the mouse over the scene to rotate the view and use the wheel to zoom in. With the headset, walk with the left joystick, turn with the right one, and use the menu on your left: point and pull the trigger. Each station has a panel with the equations and a graph of the function, and you can move the variable of the problem to see how everything changes at once. You can repeat this explanation whenever you want, or turn the narration off with the narration button.
textos.rio: This is the model of the river and cable problem. A power plant stands on one bank of a river one hundred meters wide, and the factory is five hundred meters upstream, on the opposite bank. The cable can first run along the bank, at ninety pesos per meter, and then cross the water diagonally, at one hundred and fifty pesos per meter. The variable x is the stretch that runs along the bank. Drag the orange post on the model, move the slider or the point on the graph, and watch how the two stretches and the total cost change. The endpoint buttons take the post to x equal to zero and to x equal to five hundred, so you can compare those costs with the minimum. With Go to real scale you will walk through the valley at its true size. When you have your answer, compare it with Reveal solution, and remember that the problem asks for the length of the cable route.
textos.rio_real: Now you are in the valley, at real scale. The river is one hundred meters wide and the factory is five hundred meters upstream, on the other bank. The orange line along the bank is the stretch of cable over land, and the dashed line crosses the water to the factory. The orange post marks the point where the cable leaves the bank. Move it with the slider or with the graph, and see how the length and the cost of each stretch change. With the headset, the left joystick takes you quickly through the valley, and the right one lets you rise to look at it from above. With Back to the model you return to the table.
textos.cisterna: This is the minimum-cost cistern. It must hold twelve thousand cubic decimeters of water, and its base and lid are square. The concrete for the base and the sides costs one hundred pesos per square decimeter, and the material for the lid costs twice as much. The variable x is the side of the base. Since the volume is fixed, the height adjusts by itself every time you change x. Drag the orange sphere, move the slider or the point on the graph, and watch how the shape of the cistern and the total cost change. With Lift the lid you can look inside. When you think you have found the minimum, check it with Go to optimum or with Reveal solution.
textos.caja: In this workshop an open-top box is made from a square piece of cardboard twenty-four inches on a side. A square of side x is cut from each corner, and then the edges are folded up. If you cut a little, the box is very shallow, and if you cut a lot, the base gets smaller. Drag the orange sphere at the corner, move the slider or the point on the graph, and see how the volume changes. With Unfold you see the flat cardboard with the cuts, and with Fill with sand you can compare the volumes of different boxes. Finally, check your result with Go to optimum or with Reveal solution.
textos.arena: Here an open-top container is built to store ten cubic meters of sand. The length of the base is twice its width. The bottom costs thirty thousand pesos per square meter, and the sides, twenty thousand. The variable is the width of the base, which we call w. When you change it, the height adjusts by itself to keep the volume. A small base forces very tall sides, and a large base makes the bottom expensive. Drag the orange sphere, move the slider or the point on the graph, and look for the lowest cost. With Show sand you see the material inside the container. Then check it with Go to optimum or with Reveal solution.
textos.postes: Here there are two poles, one twelve feet and the other twenty-eight feet high, thirty feet apart. Each pole is held by a cable that runs down to the same stake driven into the ground between them. The variable x is the distance from the stake to the shorter pole. Drag the orange stake, move the slider or the point on the graph, and watch how the total length of cable changes. The endpoint button takes the stake to the foot of one of the poles, so you can compare the endpoints of the interval with the minimum. Notice also the angle that each cable makes with the ground. Then check your result with Go to optimum or with Reveal solution.
textos.ondas: A person throws a stone into the lake and circular ripples form. The radius of the outer circle grows at a constant rate of one foot per second. The orange circle is the wave front, and the light-blue layer is the area it encloses. Use Throw the stone to see the throw, Play to make time move forward, or move the time slider. Notice that the radius always grows at the same pace, but the area does not. On the area graph, the slope of the tangent is the rate at which the area grows. With Go to r equals four feet you reach the instant of the problem. The panel keeps that rate hidden until you turn on Reveal answer.
textos.aviones: On this air traffic control desk you can see two airplanes flying at the same altitude, on perpendicular routes that cross at point O. One is two hundred and twenty-five miles from O and flies at four hundred and fifty miles per hour. The other is three hundred miles away and flies at six hundred. Play the clock or move the time to see how they approach each other, and adjust the clock speed if you need to. On the graph of the distance between the airplanes, the slope of the tangent is the rate at which that distance changes. With Go to the instant you place yourself at the moment of the problem, and with Reveal answer you check your calculation. If you keep moving time forward, you will see what happens when both reach point O.
textos.grava: A conveyor belt discharges gravel at a rate of thirty cubic feet per minute, and the pile forms a cone whose base diameter is always equal to its height. Play the time or move the slider to watch the pile grow. Although the gravel falls at a constant rate, notice whether the height always rises equally fast. On the height graph, the slope of the tangent is the rate at which the pile rises. With Go to h equals ten feet you reach the instant of the problem. The panel keeps that rate hidden until you turn on Reveal answer.
textos.escalera: A thirteen-meter ladder leans against the wall of the building and starts to slide. Its base moves away from the wall at five meters per second. Play the slide or move the time, and watch how the top comes down. Besides the height, the problem asks about the area of the triangle formed by the ladder, the ground and the wall, and about the angle of the ladder with the ground. On the height graph, the slope of the curve is the rate at which the ladder comes down. With Go to x equals twelve meters you reach the instant of the problem. The three rates stay hidden in the panel until you turn on Reveal answer.
textos.deposito: This tank has the shape of a cone with its vertex down. It is ten meters high and has a radius of fifteen meters. Water flows out through the vertex at one cubic meter per second, and water flows in through the pipe at a constant rate, which we call c. The problem asks for the inflow c that makes the level rise at four meters per second, at the instant when the water is one meter deep. Move the inflow and the level with the sliders, drag the light-blue sphere, or turn on Simulate to watch the tank fill. Look for the inflow with which the curve on the graph passes through the guide of four meters per second, exactly at one meter of depth. With Go to h equals one meter and with Reveal you check your result.
textos.autos: From this tower you see two roads that cross. One car travels east at ninety kilometers per hour, and another travels south at sixty, and both are heading toward the intersection. Play the time or move the slider to watch them advance. The distances from each car to the intersection decrease, and that is why their derivatives are negative. The graph shows the distance between the two cars, and the slope of its tangent is the rate at which they approach each other. With Go to the instant you place yourself at the moment when the first car is two hundred meters from the intersection and the second is one hundred and fifty. Then turn on Reveal answer to check your calculation.
